content.objectives: Use union, intersection and complement; partition a two-set Venn diagram; apply inclusion–exclusion without double-counting.
content.reading:
OFFICIAL ALIGNMENT
REB Senior 1 Mathematics, Unit 1 set operations.

SUPERTEACHER DEEP EXPLANATION
Set operations act like filters. Intersection means both rules must pass. Union means at least one rule passes. Complement reverses a rule, but only inside a stated universal set.
content.deep_explanation:
INTERSECTION = AND
If A is multiples of 2 and B is multiples of 3, A ∩ B contains multiples of 6.

UNION = INCLUSIVE OR
A ∪ B includes A-only, B-only and the overlap.

COMPLEMENT NEEDS U
If U={1,…,10} and A is the evens, Aᶜ={1,3,5,7,9}.

WHY INCLUSION–EXCLUSION WORKS
n(A)+n(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract n(A∩B) once.
content.examples: In a class of 48, 29 study French, 26 study Kiswahili and 8 study neither. Forty study at least one language. Therefore 40=29+26−both, so 15 study both.
content.practice:
1. Let U={1,…,12}, A be multiples of 2 and B multiples of 3. Find A∩B, A∪B and Aᶜ.
2. Of 60 learners, 35 play football, 28 basketball and 12 both. How many play neither?
3. Explain why A∩B ⊆ A∪B.
content.practice_answers:
1. A∩B={6,12}; A∪B={2,3,4,6,8,9,10,12}; Aᶜ={1,3,5,7,9,11}.
2. At least one=35+28−12=51, so neither=9.
3. Anything in both sets is certainly in at least one.
content.summary: Think in disjoint regions. Add each region once. State the universal set before using a complement.

quiz.question: Why is n(A∩B) subtracted in the two-set union formula?

content.checkbox_answers:
☐ I filled the overlap before the A-only and B-only regions.
☐ My disjoint regions add to the universal total.
☐ I did not count the overlap twice.
content.experiment: Survey at least 20 classmates about two activities. Predict the overlap, draw the Venn diagram, then verify all regions sum to the sample size.
content.assignment: Create consistent three-set transport data for 60 students and write three inclusion–exclusion questions with worked solutions.
